terms.definition: Tacked onto a verb, says something can't happen because of circumstances or capacity, not because it's forbidden: too much to eat, too late to go. /tɕʰy˥˩ pu liau˨˩˦/
terms.example: 菜点太多了，我们两个人吃不了。 — We ordered too much; the two of us can't finish it.
terms.anti_example: Too full to finish? Say 吃不了, not 不能吃: 不能吃 means the food isn't safe or you aren't allowed to eat it.

terms.definition: Says 'no wonder': you've just learned the reason, and something that puzzled you now makes sense. /nan˧˥ kuai˥˩/
terms.example: 他有孩子了？难怪最近总是这么累。 — He had a baby? No wonder he's so tired lately.

terms.definition: Tells you something came very close to happening but in the end didn't: 'almost', 'nearly'. /ʈʂʰa˥˩ tiɐɻ˨˩˦/
terms.example: 今天在地铁站楼梯上差点儿摔倒。 — I nearly fell on the subway stairs today.
terms.controversy: People disagree over 差点儿没. With bad events, 差点儿没摔倒 still means 'almost fell'; some teachers call that illogical, but speakers use it daily. Safe default: plain 差点儿.

terms.definition: Disagrees gently: 'not necessarily', 'I wouldn't be so sure'. Softer than telling someone they're wrong. /pu˧˥ tɕiɛn˥˩ tɤ˧˥/
terms.example: 贵的饭馆不见得更好吃。 — Expensive restaurants aren't necessarily better.
terms.discussion: Close to 不一定, but it sounds more like your own doubt. It also works alone as a reply: 他会来吧？ — 不见得。

terms.definition: Puts the most extreme, least expected case in front of the verb to say 'even X', usually in surprise or complaint. /liɛn˧˥ wo˨˩ tou˥/
terms.example: 他忙得连饭都没时间吃。 — He's so busy he doesn't even have time to eat.
terms.discussion: 连……也 works the same way. The whole 连 phrase goes before the verb; English speakers tend to leave 'even' where English puts it, and drop the 都.

terms.definition: Waves away the details: whatever the situation, the result won't change, so act on that. Often comes with a shrug or mild impatience. /fan˨˩ ʈʂəŋ˥˩/
terms.example: 反正已经迟到了，别打车了，坐地铁吧。 — We're late anyway, so forget the taxi; let's take the subway.
terms.anti_example: English 'Anyway, how was your trip?' isn't 反正: to change the subject, use 对了. 反正 always means the outcome stays the same whatever happens.

terms.definition: Can't bring yourself to let go: to leave a person or place, throw something out, or spend money on it. /ʂɤ˨˩ pu tə/
terms.example: 我妈舍不得扔这件旧大衣。 — My mom can't bear to throw out this old coat.
terms.anti_example: 舍不得买 means you won't let yourself spend; 买不起 means you really can't afford it. English 'I can't afford it' is usually 买不起.

terms.definition: Stresses that something finally happened only after a lot of trouble: 'at long last', 'it took forever, but'. /xau˨˩ pu˥˩ ʐʊŋ˧˥ i˥˩/
terms.example: 春节的火车票我好不容易才买到。 — It took forever, but I finally got Spring Festival train tickets.
terms.discussion: Usually followed by 才 + verb. Oddly, 好容易才买到 means exactly the same, so don't read the 不 as 'not'.

terms.definition: Starts from a fact both speakers already accept and draws the obvious next step: 'since that's so, then…'. Handy for nudging a decision. /tɕi˥˩ ʐan˧˥ lei˥˩ lə tɕiou˥˩ ʂuei˥˩/
terms.example: 既然你这么累，就别去聚会了。 — Since you're this tired, skip the party.
terms.anti_example: Not 既然 for news the listener doesn't know yet: 因为下雨，我没去 explains a reason. 既然 only builds on a fact already on the table.

terms.definition: Presses for a straight answer in a question, like 'on earth' or 'exactly': you've waited long enough. /tau˥˩ ti˨˩˦/
terms.example: 你到底想吃什么？ — What on earth do you want to eat?
terms.anti_example: Never with 吗: 你到底去不去？ or 你到底去哪儿？, not 你到底去吗？ 到底 needs a question word or an A-not-A choice.
terms.discussion: It can sound impatient, so soften it with 呢 and avoid it with your boss. Outside questions it also means 'after all' (他到底是孩子) or 'to the end' (坚持到底).
